prompt: What is wrong with picturing team freedom as one slider from “manager decides” to “team decides”?
hint: How many axes did Kniberg draw?

choices.text: It makes autonomy and alignment opposites, when they are independent
choices.why: Right: on two axes, a team can have more of both at once.

choices.text: It leaves out the team’s product manager
choices.why: The picture is about who decides and who knows the goal, not about roles.

choices.text: Teams have no autonomy anyway
choices.why: The lesson treats autonomy as real and worth having, at a price.

choices.text: It puts the manager at one end, when the manager should sit in the middle of every decision the team makes
choices.why: Sitting in the middle of every decision is the bottleneck lesson 3 warned against.

prompt: Match each corner of Kniberg’s grid with what the manager says in it.
hint: Goal explained or not; solution chosen or not.

pairs.right: “we need to cross; build this bridge, this way”
“we need to cross, and this is why”

prompt: A manager wants to give the team more autonomy. On the two axes, what should change in what they say?
hint: The total does not go down; it moves.

choices.text: Less overall, so the team has room to think for itself
choices.why: Saying less overall is the slider picture, and it leaves the team without the goal.

choices.text: Nothing; autonomy is about trust, not words
choices.why: The lesson describes the price of aligned autonomy as the manager’s effort explaining the problem.

choices.text: More about the method, so mistakes are avoided
choices.why: That moves the team towards the authoritative corner, with less autonomy.

choices.text: More about the goal, less about the method
choices.why: Right: communication moves from how to why, and the team decides the how.

prompt: Why did Renata ask Otávio for the problem instead of accepting his list of three features?

choices.text: She thought the three features were wrong and wanted to replace them with her own
choices.why: She did not reject them; two shipped later, and she called them ideas rather than a plan.

choices.text: The list chose the solution for the team, while the problem left the team free to find one
choices.why: Right, and the team then found that most no-shows came from bookings made weeks ahead, which none of the three targeted.

choices.text: Because a manager should never accept a list from above
choices.why: Nothing says that; the point is which corner of the grid the list put the team in.

choices.text: To delay the quarter until there was more data
choices.why: Gathering more before acting is the instinct against the knowledge gap that the next section warns about.

prompt: Agenda’s data says about one appointment in nine is a no-show. Out of 900 appointments, about how many is that?
Which gap is between what people do and what it achieves?
hint: The work was done as intended.

choices.text: Effects
choices.why: Right: actions done as planned that do not have the effect planned.

choices.text: Knowledge, between the plan and what is really out there
choices.why: That one is between plans and outcomes: planning on incomplete information.

choices.text: Alignment, between the plan and what people do
choices.why: That one is people doing something other than what was meant.

choices.text: Communication
choices.why: Not one of Bungay’s three.

prompt: What do the three instinctive responses to Bungay’s gaps have in common?

choices.text: Each moves decisions down to the team
choices.why: The instincts do the opposite and pull decisions up.

choices.text: Each one works for a while, until the team grows past about ten people and the gap returns
choices.why: Bungay’s point is that they make the gap worse, not that they stop working at some size.

choices.text: Each adds detail, and widens the gap it meant to close
choices.why: Right: more information, more instructions, more controls, and less room to respond.

choices.text: Each is what Bungay recommends
choices.why: He recommends the opposite of each: decide only what you must, explain intent, give freedom to adjust.

prompt: Match each gap with what Bungay recommends against it.

pairs.right: decide only what you must, at your level
explain the intent rather than add instructions
give people freedom to adjust within limits

right_distractors: add a weekly report against a target

prompt: Freed slots late in the day stayed empty after the cancellation link shipped. Why did the plan change without anybody issuing an instruction?
hint: What did the team know the plan was for?

choices.text: Otávio added a weekly target for slot reuse
choices.why: That was the instinct the lesson describes, and it did not happen.

choices.text: The clinics fixed it themselves
choices.why: The clinics complained; the team changed the product.

choices.text: The team knew the goal was appointments kept, so it moved the waiting list up
choices.why: Right: knowing the intent let the people who saw the effects gap act on it.

choices.text: Renata decided it alone and told the team
choices.why: She shared the complaint and the goal; the team chose the waiting list.

prompt: By the Amazon letter’s distinction, where do two-way doors belong?
hint: A wrong decision is cheap to undo.

choices.text: With the most senior person available
choices.why: That treats a two-way door as a one-way door, which the letter warns makes everything slow.

choices.text: In a design review across teams
choices.why: That is for consequential one-way doors, like changing the database engine.

choices.text: As close to the work as possible
choices.why: Right: the cost of a wrong decision is small and the cost of waiting is not.

choices.text: With whoever will live with the consequences longest, after a formal written review of the options
choices.why: That is where one-way doors go.

prompt: A new public API field looks easy to rename on the day it ships. Why does the lesson warn against treating it as a two-way door?
hint: What happens to it over the next six months?

choices.text: Things get built on it, and it hardens
choices.why: Right: clinics’ systems start calling it, and six months later the rename is expensive.

choices.text: APIs are never allowed to change
choices.why: They change; the cost of changing grows with what depends on them.

choices.text: Field names need the legal team’s approval
choices.why: Legal approved the reminder text, not API fields.

choices.text: Because the team has no right to make technical decisions about anything clinics will see
choices.why: Nothing removes the team’s right; the question is how reversible the decision really is.

prompt: At three in the morning, nobody knew who could turn off a feature flag. What does the lesson draw from it?
hint: Some owners can be found over a week; some cannot.

choices.text: Write down first the decisions needed in a hurry
choices.why: Right: a rollback owner cannot be worked out while customers are failing to book.

choices.text: Feature flags should only be turned off by the tech lead
choices.why: The lesson does not assign the flag to Diego; it says the decision had no owner.

choices.text: On-call engineers should wake the manager for every decision
choices.why: That is the twenty-minute wait, made a rule.

choices.text: Incidents are too rare to plan decision rights for
choices.why: The lesson argues the opposite: hurried decisions are the ones most worth writing down.

prompt: A decision that is consequential and hard to reverse is called a ___-way door.
Renata’s decisions page shows her own name on nine of the last ten lines. Which conclusions does the lesson support? Choose all that apply.
hint: What does one name on most lines mean?

choices.text: The page should stop recording who decided
choices.why: No: that column is what revealed the pattern.

choices.text: Some two-way doors are probably being decided too far from the work
choices.why: Yes: two-way doors belong close to the work.

choices.text: The team has less autonomy than she thinks
choices.why: Yes: the lesson says exactly this about a page where every line says “Renata”.

choices.text: She is doing her job well, since a manager should decide most things
choices.why: No: by lessons 3 and 4, that makes her the bottleneck.

prompt: A director tells a team: “Reduce checkout failures by half this quarter. Here is why it matters, here is what you may not touch, and here is the dashboard.” The team asks which fix to build. Which corner of Kniberg’s grid is the director aiming at, and what is missing?
hint: Is the problem the goal, or the team expecting a solution?

choices.text: High alignment and low autonomy; she should choose the fix
choices.why: Choosing the fix would move the team to the authoritative corner, which she deliberately avoided.

choices.text: Aligned autonomy; the team has yet to take up the “how”
choices.why: Right: the four things alignment needs are there, and the remaining step is the team deciding the method.

choices.text: Low alignment and high autonomy; the goal is too vague
choices.why: The goal has a measure, a reason, limits and a dashboard, which is not vague.

choices.text: Low on both axes
choices.why: The goal is explained thoroughly, so alignment is high.
